name: Generalists unlock income specialists cannot
definition: Specialists have an income ceiling because their narrow expertise limits what they can see and do. Generalists who develop competence across multiple skills discover opportunities at the intersections between domains—where the real money is made.
core_claim: If you develop competence across multiple skills rather than mastering just one, then you unlock income and opportunities unavailable to specialists, because value compounds at the intersections between domains, not within them.

idea_origin.event_summary: Worked as a writer focused solely on improving writing skills. Watched boss Jariah suddenly start making significantly more money. Asked what changed—he explained that learning all the skills (management, sales, strategy) even ones he didn't enjoy was what unlocked it.
idea_origin.trigger: Jariah said 'specialists have an income cap' and 'the money is really made between each vertical, not within them.'
idea_origin.lesson_learned: Stopped identifying solely as a writer. Learned crypto strategy, prompt engineering, bot creation, metrics analysis. Became the last remaining contractor because of the complete package, not just writing ability.

canonical_instruction: Identify the primary skill the writer is relying on. Then identify 2-3 adjacent skills that would create leverage when combined with the primary skill. Reframe the value proposition from 'I am good at X' to 'I can deliver the complete outcome by combining X + Y + Z.' Show how the intersections between skills create opportunities invisible to single-skill specialists.

situations: when afraid to learn new skills
exclusions: fields requiring deep specialization by law (surgery, law)
early skill-building phase where fundamentals matter
contexts where generalism signals lack of expertise

transformation_rules: Identify the writer's primary skill or identity
List adjacent skills that would compound with the primary skill
Reframe value from single-skill to multi-skill package
Show where 'money between verticals' applies to their situation
Add a 'get hands dirty' example—an uncomfortable skill worth learning
Surface the income ceiling of remaining a pure specialist
tests: Output names at least 2 adjacent skills to learn
Output reframes identity from specialist to generalist
Output contains phrase about intersections or connections between skills
Output acknowledges discomfort of learning new skills is worth it
No language suggesting 'just get better at your one thing'
Reader can identify one concrete skill to add to their stack
counterexamples: Medical specialization where generalism is dangerous (you want a heart surgeon, not a general doctor)
Early career when you haven't mastered any skill yet—foundation first, then expand
Contexts where being a 'jack of all trades' signals incompetence rather than versatility
input_triggers: identifying too strongly with one skill
watching others succeed with less raw skill
asking 'how do I make more money'

related.note: Related to 'get hands dirty' principle about willingness to do uncomfortable work
Related to identity flexibility—willingness to become someone new to unlock new skills

components.name: Get hands dirty on uncomfortable skills
